unit-m3-review.title: Unit 3 · Test Review: Check Your Work
unit-m3-review.source: Math update (teacher) and the Unit 3 textbook scan

summary.text: A test review for Unit 3: finding the mistake in a wrong multiplication, and four quick ways to check your own answer before you hand it in.

why.text: Your teacher says most mistakes on this test are simple slips, not missing skills. Catching your own slip before the test does is the whole skill here.

objectives.text: Find and name the mistake in a wrong multiplication.
Check an answer with an estimate, the ones digit, the zeros, or division.
Decide whether an answer to a story problem is reasonable.

parentNote.text: Built from the teacher's math update for the Unit 3 test on Tuesday 10/20. She asks families to practise double-checking and to "give them a problem that is wrong and see if they can find the mistake", so this review is mostly that: twelve find-the-mistake and which-check-catches-it items, plus products to choose and two story problems. Every wrong answer comes from a named slip (a dropped carry, products written side by side, the missing zero in the second row, a skipped zero, a lost zero with powers of ten). Her paper study guide (handed out Friday 10/16) is not in Drive, so this does not mirror it; it uses fresh numbers on the nine lessons' skills. Worth approving today if she is to see it before the test.

nextUp.text: Take one round tonight, and for every mistake you catch, say out loud which check found it.

cards.def:
**Most mistakes on a multiplication test are slips, not "I do not know how".**
• A carry forgotten, a zero left off, two numbers copied wrong.
• A minute of checking catches most of them.
cards.hint: Know the skill, then guard it.

cards.def:
**Round both numbers and multiply. The real answer should be close.**
• 68 × 42 → 70 × 40 = 2,800. An answer of 286 or 28,560 is far off.
• An estimate catches a lost or extra place, not a small slip.
cards.hint: Too big or too small by a lot? Something went wrong.

cards.def:
**The ones digit of the answer comes only from the two ones digits.**
• 46 × 23: 6 × 3 = 18, so the answer must end in 8.
• If your answer ends in anything else, there is a slip.
cards.hint: Last digits make the last digit.

cards.def:
**When you multiply by 10, 100 or 1,000, count the zeros on both sides.**
• 60 × 4,000: one zero plus three zeros is four zeros: 240,000.
• If the basic fact already ends in 0 (5 × 8 = 40), that zero is extra.
cards.hint: Zeros in, zeros out, plus any the fact makes.

cards.def:
**Division undoes multiplication: divide your answer by one factor, and you should get the other.**
• 125 × 8 = 1,000, so 1,000 ÷ 8 should be 125.

**Writing only the ones digit of a step and forgetting to carry the tens.**
• 47 × 6: 7 × 6 = 42, write 2, carry 4. 4 × 6 = 24, plus 4 is 28. Answer 282.
• Forgetting the carry gives 242.
cards.hint: Every carry has to be added somewhere.

cards.def:
**Writing each part's whole product next to the others instead of adding by place.**
• 38 × 4: 3 × 4 = 12 and 8 × 4 = 32 written as 1,232. The real answer is 152.
cards.hint: Products go in place value, not in a row.

cards.def:
**In the second row of a 2-digit multiplication you are multiplying by TENS, so it needs a 0 in the ones place.**
• 43 × 27: 43 × 7 = 301, and 43 × 20 = 860, not 86.
• 301 + 860 = 1,161. Forgetting the zero gives 387.
cards.hint: The tens row starts with a zero.

cards.def:
**A zero inside a number still holds a place.**
• 507 × 6 is 3,042. Treating 507 like 57 gives 342.
cards.hint: Zeros hold places, even when they make nothing.

cards.def:
**Redo the problem step by step and compare each line with the one written.**
• The first line that does not match is where the mistake is.
• Then name it: a carry, a zero, a wrong fact, or a split that does not add up.
cards.hint: Find the first line that differs.

cards.def:
**Write every row, every carry and every partial product.**
• Work you can see is work you can check, and homework is marked on it.
cards.hint: If it is not written, it cannot be checked.

questions.q: Jada worked out 47 × 6 and wrote 242. What went wrong?
opts: They forgot to add a carry
They wrote each part's product side by side
They left the zero off the second row
They skipped the zero inside a number
questions.hint: Work the ones step and look at what it carries.
steps: 7 × 6 = 42: write 2 and carry 4.
4 × 6 = 24, plus the carried 4 is 28.
The carry was dropped.

ex.main: **They forgot to add a carry.** 47 × 6 is 282.
ex.tip: Check the ones digit too: it is right, which is why only the carry is wrong.

questions.q: Ben worked out 58 × 7 and wrote 356. What went wrong?
opts: They wrote each part's product side by side
They forgot to add a carry
They left the zero off the second row
They skipped the zero inside a number
questions.hint: Work the ones step and look at what it carries.
steps: 8 × 7 = 56: write 6 and carry 5.
5 × 7 = 35, plus the carried 5 is 40.
The carry was dropped.

ex.main: **They forgot to add a carry.** 58 × 7 is 406.
ex.tip: Check the ones digit too: it is right, which is why only the carry is wrong.

questions.q: Leo worked out 38 × 4 and wrote 1,232. What went wrong?
opts: They forgot to add a carry
They left the zero off the second row
They wrote each part's product side by side
They skipped the zero inside a number
questions.hint: Look at the two parts and where they were written.
steps: Those were written next to each other: 1,232.
The tens part is 12 tens, so add by place: 120 + 32 = 152.
They wrote the products side by side.

ex.main: **They wrote each part's product side by side.** 38 × 4 is 152.
ex.tip: An estimate catches it fast: 38 × 4 is near 160, not 1,232.

questions.q: Mia worked out 29 × 6 and wrote 1,254. What went wrong?
opts: They forgot to add a carry
They skipped the zero inside a number
They left the zero off the second row
They wrote each part's product side by side
questions.hint: Look at the two parts and where they were written.
steps: Those were written next to each other: 1,254.
The tens part is 12 tens, so add by place: 120 + 54 = 174.
They wrote the products side by side.

ex.main: **They wrote each part's product side by side.** 29 × 6 is 174.
ex.tip: An estimate catches it fast: 29 × 6 is near 180, not 1,254.

questions.q: Sam worked out 43 × 27 and wrote 387. What went wrong?
opts: They left the zero off the second row
They wrote each part's product side by side
They forgot to add a carry
They skipped the zero inside a number
questions.hint: What should the second row be worth?
steps: First row: 43 × 7 = 301.
Second row: 43 × 20 = 860. It is multiplying by tens.
They wrote 86 instead of 860, leaving off the zero.

ex.main: **They left the zero off the second row.** 43 × 27 is 1,161.
ex.tip: The estimate 40 × 30 = 1,200 shows 387 is far too small.

questions.q: Ava worked out 52 × 36 and wrote 468. What went wrong?
opts: They forgot to add a carry
They left the zero off the second row
They wrote each part's product side by side
They skipped the zero inside a number
questions.hint: What should the second row be worth?
steps: First row: 52 × 6 = 312.
Second row: 52 × 30 = 1,560. It is multiplying by tens.
They wrote 156 instead of 1,560, leaving off the zero.

ex.main: **They left the zero off the second row.** 52 × 36 is 1,872.
ex.tip: The estimate 50 × 40 = 2,000 shows 468 is far too small.

questions.q: Noah worked out 507 × 6 and wrote 342. What went wrong?
opts: They forgot to add a carry
They wrote each part's product side by side
They skipped the zero inside a number
They left the zero off the second row
questions.hint: Look at the middle digit of 507.
steps: 507 has a 0 in the tens place.
342 is what 57 × 6 makes, so the zero was skipped.
Hundreds: 5 × 6 = 30 hundreds. Tens: 0. Ones: 7 × 6 = 42.

ex.main: **They skipped the zero inside a number.** 507 × 6 is 3,042.
ex.tip: Estimate: 507 × 6 is about 3,000, so 342 is too small.

questions.q: Zoe worked out 803 × 4 and wrote 332. What went wrong?
opts: They forgot to add a carry
They wrote each part's product side by side
They left the zero off the second row
They skipped the zero inside a number
questions.hint: Look at the middle digit of 803.
steps: 803 has a 0 in the tens place.
332 is what 83 × 4 makes, so the zero was skipped.
Hundreds: 8 × 4 = 32 hundreds. Tens: 0. Ones: 3 × 4 = 12.

ex.main: **They skipped the zero inside a number.** 803 × 4 is 3,212.
ex.tip: Estimate: 803 × 4 is about 3,200, so 332 is too small.

questions.q: Ana says 68 × 42 = 286. Which quick check shows her answer is wrong?
opts: Estimate: 70 × 40 = 2,800, so 286 is far too small
The ones digit: 8 × 2 = 16, so the answer cannot end in 6
It is even, but 68 × 42 has to be odd
Undo it: 286 ÷ 2 should be 68
questions.hint: Which check looks at the size of the answer?
steps: 286 ends in 6, and 8 × 2 = 16 does end in 6, so the ones digit looks fine.
68 and 42 are both even, so an even answer is fine too.
286 is about ten times too small, so the estimate catches it.

ex.main: **The estimate.** 70 × 40 = 2,800, and 286 is nowhere near it.
ex.tip: A ones-digit check cannot see a missing place. An estimate can.

questions.q: Without working out the whole problem, what must the ones digit of 46 × 23 be?
questions.hint: Multiply only the two ones digits.
steps: The ones digits are 6 and 3.
The ones digit of 18 is 8.
So 46 × 23 must end in 8.

ex.main: **8.** 6 × 3 = 18, and only that step reaches the ones place. (46 × 23 = 1,058.)
ex.tip: If your answer does not end in 8, look for the slip.

questions.q: Eli says 54 × 37 = 2,008. Which quick check shows it is wrong?
opts: The ones digit: 4 × 7 = 28, so the answer cannot end in 8
It is even, but 54 × 37 has to come out odd
Undo it: 2,008 ÷ 37 should come out to 54, and it does not
Estimate: 50 × 40 = 2,000, so 2,008 is far too big
questions.hint: The answer is close to the estimate and ends in 8. What is left?
steps: 2,008 ends in 8, and 4 × 7 = 28 ends in 8, so the ones check passes.
Estimate: 50 × 40 = 2,000. 2,008 is close, so the estimate passes too.
Undo it: 37 × 54 is 1,998, so 2,008 ÷ 37 does not come out to 54.
Only undoing it, or redoing it carefully, catches this one.

ex.main: **Undo it.** 54 × 37 = 1,998, so 2,008 cannot be right, even though it ends in 8 and is near the estimate.
ex.tip: A small slip can pass the quick checks. That is why you also redo it line by line.

questions.q: Leo wrote 60 × 4,000 = 24,000. What went wrong?
opts: Nothing: 24,000 is right
He added an extra zero: the answer is 2,400
He used the wrong fact: 6 × 4 is 20
He lost one of the zeros: the answer is 240,000
questions.hint: Count the zeros in 60 and in 4,000.
steps: 60 has one zero, 4,000 has three: four zeros.
Put four zeros after 24: 240,000.
24,000 has only three, so one zero was lost.

ex.tip: Count zeros in, then make sure the same number come out.

questions.q: What is 50 × 800?
questions.hint: The fact 5 × 8 already makes a zero.
steps: 50 and 800 have three zeros between them.
Put three zeros after 40: 40,000.
The zero in 40 is extra, on top of the three.

ex.tip: Writing 4,000 means the zero inside 40 was treated as one of the three.

questions.q: Jo found that 125 × 8 = 1,000. Which fact checks it?
questions.hint: What undoes multiplying?
steps: Division undoes multiplication.
Divide the answer by one factor: 1,000 ÷ 8.
If you get the other factor, 125, the product checks.
So the check is 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125.

ex.main: **1,000 ÷ 8 = 125.** Dividing gives back the other factor.
ex.tip: 1,000 ÷ 125 would also work, but it equals 8, not 9.

questions.q: What is 76 × 8?
questions.hint: Multiply each place and carry.
steps: Write the ones digit and carry the rest.
Multiply the next place and add the carry.

ex.tip: Estimate: 76 × 8 is near 640.

questions.q: What is 409 × 7?
questions.hint: Multiply each place and carry.
steps: Write the ones digit and carry the rest.
Multiply the next place and add the carry.

ex.tip: Estimate: 409 × 7 is near 2,870.

questions.q: Which answer is correct for 312 × 19?
questions.hint: Estimate first, then check the ones digit.
steps: Estimate: about 6,000.
The ones digit must come from 2 × 9 = 18.
5,928 is near the estimate and ends in 8.

ex.main: **5,928.** It is the only option that is near 6,000 and ends in the right digit.
ex.tip: 3,120 is the missing-zero slip, and 59,280 has one place too many.

questions.q: Which answer is correct for 64 × 35?
questions.hint: Estimate first, then check the ones digit.
steps: Estimate: about 2,400.
The ones digit must come from 4 × 5 = 20.
2,240 is near the estimate and ends in 0.

ex.main: **2,240.** It is the only option that is near 2,400 and ends in the right digit.
ex.tip: 512 is the missing-zero slip, and 22,400 has one place too many.

questions.q: A school orders 24 boxes of markers with 36 markers in each box. Sam says that is 864 markers. Is that reasonable?
opts: No: 864 is too big, since 20 × 30 is only 600
No: it should be 24 + 36 = 60 markers
Yes: any answer in the hundreds is fine
questions.hint: Estimate with numbers that are easy to multiply.
steps: 24 is about 20 and 36 is about 40.
864 is close to 800.
Exact check: 24 × 36 = 864, so Sam is right.

ex.tip: Rounding both down to 20 × 30 gives a low estimate, so 864 being bigger is expected.

questions.q: A theater has 18 rows with 25 seats in each row. Priya says, "18 × 25 = 450, and 20 × 25 = 500, so 450 makes sense." Does her check make sense?
opts: No: an estimate and the real answer have to come out exactly equal
No: rounding 18 up means the real answer must be more than 500
No: she should have added 18 and 25 to check her answer instead
Yes: she rounded 18 up to 20, so the real answer should be a little less than 500
questions.hint: She rounded 18 up. Should the real answer be bigger or smaller?
steps: 18 was rounded UP to 20.
So 20 × 25 = 500 is an overestimate.
The real answer should be a little less than 500.
450 is a little less, so her check makes sense.

ex.main: **Yes.** Rounding 18 up makes 500 an overestimate, and 450 sits just under it.
ex.tip: Knowing which way you rounded tells you which side of the estimate to expect.
